cc: Fever, cough and pain on deep breathing

HPI: 25 yo m. Patient reports: The cough began 4 days ago. The discomfort is in my right lower chest. The pain stays there. It is a sharp pain when I cough or breathe deeply. The pain is 5/10. The fever began the next day and the cough is getting worse. My coworker had a respiratory illness last week. Acetaminophen lowers the fever for a few hours. Coughing and deep breathing worsen the pain. I took acetaminophen 500 mg twice yesterday. I have not had an episode like this before. I cough up yellow sputum. I am short of breath on stairs. Patient perspective: Could I give this to the people at home?

Allergies: Amoxicillin caused pruritic hives at age 17; no swelling or breathing difficulty.

FH: My mother is fifty-two and she has asthma.; My father is fifty-five and he has high blood pressure.; I have one sister, she's twenty-seven and she's healthy.

Vitals: T 101.3 F oral, P 102 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg, R 22 rpm, Pulse Ox 95% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Tired appearing, alert and oriented, speaking full sentences.

Heart: Regular tachycardia without murmur.

Lungs: Focal inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right posterior base. Dullness over the right posterior base compared with the left. Tactile fremitus is increased at the right posterior base.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Obtain chest x-ray and assess oxygenation, respiratory rate and severity to decide disposition; consider guideline-directed antibiotics after confirming the working diagnosis and review of the amoxicillin-hives history and comorbidities; explain hydration and warning signs; reassess within 48–72 hours, sooner for worsening dyspnea, confusion or inability to drink. Use large-print instructions and ask the patient to explain the medication and safety plan back.

2. Assess thromboembolic risk and use a validated diagnostic pathway if suspicion remains; obtain appropriate imaging rather than dismissing PE because fever is present; arrange urgent evaluation for clinical deterioration. If pulmonary embolism remains a concern, arrange emergency-department assessment; explain that fever does not rule out a clot and that increasing breathlessness or fainting requires immediate help.

3. Review smoking and persistent symptoms; ensure follow-up imaging or specialist evaluation if symptoms or consolidation do not resolve; offer smoking-cessation support and explain that cancer is a differential, not an established diagnosis.
